note: Repair catalog for engine/repair.ps1. Doctrine: every repair is detect -> fix -> verify, where detect and verify are the SAME read-only probe (engine/health.ps1, or a local read-only check for categories health.ps1 does not cover). A repair refuses to run when detection says the subsystem is healthy AND when detection FAILED (a broken probe is not permission to fix blind) — both overridable with -Force. whatItRuns lists the exact commands, honestly, and is positionally identical — LINE BY LINE, as text — to the step commands the engine emits for a DEFAULT invocation (no -SourcePath, -DnsProvider at its default). 'repair.ps1 -Action selftest' enforces exactly that and nothing weaker: it builds every step list, normalises only tokens whose value legitimately varies per machine or per run (%SystemRoot% / %ProgramData% / %TEMP% and their expansions, matched case-insensitively; the backup <timestamp>; runs of whitespace), and then compares character-for-character, case-sensitively. selftest prints the normalisation rules it applied in whatItRunsIntegrity.normalization, and any divergence is listed with both texts and fails the test. It used to compare command COUNTS only, which is why eleven repairs had drifted; a matching count is no longer a pass. Non-default switches change what runs (correctly — -SourcePath adds /Source /LimitAccess, -DnsProvider selects a different resolver pair), and 'repair.ps1 -Action preflight' renders those exact commands. reversible=false repairs record what was renamed/moved in the repair ledger (renames use .bak-<timestamp> names, moves go to the backups folder beside it, so manual recovery stays possible) — see stateLocationNote for where that is and why it is NOT in the install tree. restorePoint='enforced' means a System Restore checkpoint is created as the FIRST step and the repair ABORTS if it cannot be created; -NoRestorePoint is the explicit opt-out. Unlike WinUtil, NOTHING in this catalog deletes Policies hives, GroupPolicy folders, or runs secedit.
regsvr32Note: WinUtil's Windows Update reset re-registers 36 DLLs with regsvr32 (atl, urlmon, mshtml, wuapi, wuaueng, qmgr, ...). FrameForge deliberately does NOT: that block is a Windows XP/Vista-era ritual for a servicing stack that no longer exists. On Windows 10/11 those components are registered by the component store (WinSxS) and protected by Windows Resource Protection; regsvr32 against them either no-ops or fails, and the real fix for a genuinely broken registration is DISM/SFC, which this catalog offers directly (dism-restorehealth). Running 36 pointless regsvr32 calls to look thorough would be exactly the placebo behaviour FrameForge exists to avoid.
restorePointNote: winutil-dissection.md section 8 names 'enforced restore points' as a beatable dimension: WinUtil's restore point is an opt-in checkbox in a tweak list. Here it is enforced-by-default for every aggressive-tier repair plus winsock-reset, created BEFORE the first mutation, recorded in the ledger with its sequence number, and surfaced in preflight. If System Protection is off and the checkpoint cannot be created, the repair aborts instead of running unprotected. The checkpoint step has to bypass Windows' once-per-24h restore-point throttle (SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency=0) to be sure it actually gets a checkpoint — and that bypass is TEMPORARY: the prior value, or the fact that the value did not exist, is captured first and put back in a finally block, so it is restored even when Checkpoint-Computer itself fails. Both the set and the restore appear in the run's mutation record, and a restore that fails is reported loudly instead of swallowed. Leaving that value at 0 behind would be a permanent, system-wide change made by the one step whose entire purpose is safety.
resultFieldsNote: A run's result object reports stepsCompleted (every step that counts ran without error), verified (the same read-only probe that detected the problem now reports healthy), and addressed (both — the only one of the three that means the problem is gone). 'fixed' is retained as a DEPRECATED alias of stepsCompleted for the existing UI renderer and must not be read by new code: steps completing is not the same as the finding being resolved. spooler-clear-queue is the worked example — it claims the printer-error-state finding, but a printer that is simply Offline is not something clearing the spool queue can fix, so every step can succeed while the printer stays offline. verified is what catches that.
optionalFeaturesNote: WinUtil's Features tab (winutil-dissection.md section 3.8) installs a mixed bag of Windows optional features. FrameForge implements the ones that are genuinely REPAIR-shaped — where the symptom is 'this application will not start' and enabling the feature is the fix: enable-netfx3 (.NET Framework 3.5, which carries 2.0 and 3.0), enable-netfx4-advsrvs (.NET Framework 4.x advanced services / WCF activation), and enable-directplay (the legacy DirectPlay runtime a lot of pre-2010 games still call). Each has real detection (Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online), captures the exact prior State, and has a real undo (Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature, with -Remove when the captured state was DisabledWithPayloadRemoved). DELIBERATELY NOT DONE, with reasons rather than silence: Hyper-V (Microsoft-Hyper-V-All), WSL (VirtualMachinePlatform + Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux), Windows Sandbox (Containers-DisposableClientVM) and the NFS client are capability ADDITIONS, not repairs — nothing is broken before you enable them, there is no fault to detect and nothing to verify afterwards, and Hyper-V in particular silently changes how the machine boots (it turns on the hypervisor, which measurably affects games and is a thing FrameForge would then have to argue about). Windows Media Player / MediaPlayback / LegacyComponents beyond DirectPlay are likewise preferences, not faults. WinUtil's daily registry-backup task (EnablePeriodicBackup=1, BackupCount=2, a scheduled task firing RegIdleBackup at 00:30) is a preventive configuration change that installs a permanent scheduled task and grows the registry backup set forever — a defensible thing to want, but it repairs nothing and FrameForge does not install standing tasks on a machine to fix a problem that has not happened. WinUtil's legacy F8 boot menu (bcdedit /set bootmenupolicy legacy) is a boot-configuration preference; FrameForge does not write BCD, because a mistake there costs a boot rather than a setting. If any of these is wanted, Windows' own 'Turn Windows features on or off' is the right place, and saying so is more honest than shipping buttons that pretend a missing feature was a fault.
probeDepthNote: PROBE DEPTH, AND WHAT THE DEEP PROBE COSTS. `probeDeep: true` on a repair tells repair.ps1 to detect (and verify) that repair with health.ps1's DEEP probe for its category instead of the fast one. It is set where the fast probe structurally cannot see the fault the repair fixes. On system-files the fast probe reads only the component store's corruption FLAG (Repair-WindowsImage -CheckHealth reports what an earlier servicing operation RECORDED; it does not scan) plus the pending-reboot key, while the findings sfc-scannow, dism-restorehealth and wu-repair-reinstall key on - 'sfc-verify-violations' and 'component-store-scanhealth' - are emitted ONLY by the deep probe (sfc /verifyonly and DISM ScanHealth). Without probeDeep those three were detected by a probe that could never observe their signal: renaming a WinSxS payload file sets no flag, CheckHealth answers Healthy, and detection reported 'nothing is broken here' about corruption that was really there - doctrine rule 2's worst case, in the function that decides whether a repair runs at all. All three now declare probeDeep, so detection can actually see the fault the repair fixes. THE COST IS REAL AND IS NOT HIDDEN: the deep system-files probe runs sfc /verifyonly and DISM ScanHealth, which take minutes (roughly 2-10 on a healthy machine, longer on a slow disk) and need administrator rights - so 'repair.ps1 -Action preflight' and '-Action run' on these three repairs spend that time BEFORE anything is executed, and unelevated they report needs-admin rather than a verdict. '-Action list' deliberately does NOT pay it: listing always probes shallow and reports state 'indeterminate' with reason 'shallow-probe' for any repair marked probeDeep, so the ladder stays browsable in a second and the deciding probe runs only when you ask for that repair. Deep probes are still strictly read-only - they measure, they never repair. The same field is set on chkdsk-spotfix and chkdsk-full-repair (deep disk probe: an online chkdsk scan) and on component-cleanup and component-cleanup-resetbase (deep disk-space probe: DISM AnalyzeComponentStore). DETECTION THAT NEEDS ELEVATION (`detectionNeedsAdmin`). The same three repairs also declare detectionNeedsAdmin: true, because every finding they key on - component-store-corrupt, component-store-scanhealth and sfc-verify-violations - is emitted inside an `if ($IsAdmin)` branch of health.ps1's system-files probe. Unelevated, that probe still returns a status (a pending servicing reboot alone makes it 'warning'), and health.ps1's status rank puts warning above needs-admin, so the fact that the component-store check never ran was invisible to the repair engine: detection graded these repairs 'healthy' while quoting the sentence 'the component-store corruption check needs administrator rights; only the pending-reboot key was checked'. With the field set, a would-be healthy verdict from an unelevated run becomes indeterminate with reason 'needs-admin' - 'elevate me and I will know', never 'nothing is broken here'. It changes nothing when FrameForge is elevated, and it never downgrades a fault that was visible anyway.

repairs.name: Reset the Windows Update stack (scoped)
repairs.summary: The Microsoft-documented Windows Update component reset: re-enable disabled pipeline services, drain the BITS queue, stop the services, rename the update caches, clear a stale WinHTTP proxy and dead WSUS pinning, restart, rescan.
repairs.details: Restores the documented start type of any update-pipeline service that is DISABLED (wuauserv, BITS, CryptSvc, MSIServer, AppIDSvc, Delivery Optimization, Update Orchestrator) — a disabled service is already stopped, so without this step the whole reset is theatre and the repair would report success while changing nothing. AppIDSvc (and occasionally others) is a protected service that refuses Set-Service outright, so there is a documented second mechanism for that case only: writing the Start value directly under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name> (2 = Automatic, 3 = Manual). It is used ONLY when Set-Service has already been refused on a service detection found Disabled, the prior start type is captured either way, and the step result says which mechanism was used per service. Then: removes stuck BITS transfer jobs, stops the pipeline, moves the BITS queue database (qmgr*.dat) aside, renames SoftwareDistribution and catroot2 to timestamped .bak names (never deletes them), resets the WinHTTP proxy (a stale one is a very common cause of updates hanging at 0%), removes WSUS client-identity values that pin the machine to a dead update server (only when no live WUServer policy is set — see managedMachineNote), restarts the services, and triggers a new scan with UsoClient, checking its exit code and falling back to Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate.DetectNow() when the verb is refused or missing on this build, so a scan that could not be triggered is reported as such instead of claimed. Deliberately SCOPED: unlike WinUtil's version it never deletes Policies registry hives, never removes GroupPolicy folders, never runs secedit, and never runs the obsolete 36-DLL regsvr32 block (see regsvr32Note). Service start types, WinHTTP proxy, WSUS identity values, BITS queue files, and cache-folder state are all captured to the ledger before anything changes. A service in this set that is NOT PRESENT AT ALL fails the re-enable step rather than being noted in passing: these are core Windows client services, FrameForge cannot read or restore a start type for a service that does not exist, and a step that reports success for something it never measured is exactly what doctrine rule 2 forbids. The rest of the reset still runs; the run is simply reported as not completed.
whatItRuns: Set-Service -StartupType <documented default> on any DISABLED service among: wuauserv=Manual, bits=Manual, cryptSvc=Automatic, msiserver=Manual, appidsvc=Manual, DoSvc=Automatic, UsoSvc=Automatic  (prior start type captured to the ledger; enabled services are left alone). Fallback when Set-Service is refused on a PROTECTED service (appidsvc is the usual one): Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>' -Name Start -Value <2=Automatic|3=Manual> -Type DWord
Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers | Remove-BitsTransfer
Stop-Service -Name wuauserv, cryptSvc, bits, msiserver, appidsvc -Force
Move-Item %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\qmgr*.dat -> %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\backups\bits-queue-<timestamp>\  (moved, not deleted)
Rename-Item %SystemRoot%\SoftwareDistribution -> SoftwareDistribution.bak-<timestamp>
Rename-Item %SystemRoot%\System32\catroot2 -> catroot2.bak-<timestamp>

netsh winhttp reset proxy   (current setting captured via "netsh winhttp show proxy" in the ledger before-state; SKIPPED without running when this machine is WSUS-pinned, MDM-enrolled or domain-joined AND a proxy is actually configured — on a managed network clearing it cuts the machine off from updates rather than fixing them, and this repair is reversible:false so there would be no automatic way back)

Remove-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate' -Name AccountDomainSid, PingID, SusClientId, SusClientIdValidation  (prior values captured to the ledger; NOT run when HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\WUServer pins this machine to a live WSUS server — removing a managed client's identity is an administrator action, not a user one)
Start-Service on each service this run stopped, plus any this run re-enabled from Disabled

UsoClient.exe StartScan   (exit code checked, not discarded; when the verb is refused or missing on this build, (New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate).DetectNow() is used instead, and a scan that could not be triggered at all is reported as such)
repairs.risks: Update history display is cleared and any partially downloaded updates are downloaded again. Pending BITS transfers (including background app updates) are cancelled. On an UNMANAGED machine a configured WinHTTP proxy is cleared; the previous setting is recorded both in the ledger before-state and in the step's own mutation record, and because this repair is reversible:false there is NO automatic undo — re-apply it by hand with 'netsh winhttp set proxy "<recorded value>"'. On an unmanaged machine the WSUS client-identity values (left behind by a previous domain or a dead WSUS server) are removed and the client re-registers with Microsoft on the next scan; the prior values are recorded. The old cache folders and BITS queue files are renamed/moved (paths recorded in the ledger), not deleted, so manual recovery is possible. Group Policy, service ACLs, and unrelated settings are never touched. MANAGED MACHINES: if this machine is pinned to a WSUS server by Group Policy, is MDM-enrolled, or is domain-joined, the WinHTTP proxy reset and the WSUS client-identity removal are SKIPPED rather than executed, and each step says so by name — clearing a mandatory proxy would cut a managed PC off from updates, and removing a managed client's identity is an administrator action. When the update policy key cannot be read at all, both steps take the same cautious branch instead of guessing. 'repair.ps1 -Action preflight' shows the detected management state before you run anything.
repairs.verifyAfter: The windows-update health probe is re-run. Note: failure events from before the reset persist in the event log for their 30-day window, so the definitive confirmation is the next successful update scan (event 19) — the verify result says so honestly instead of claiming success early.

repairs.name: Reset the Windows Update stack (aggressive: + service security descriptors)
repairs.summary: Everything wu-reset does, plus restoring the default security descriptors on wuauserv and BITS — behind an enforced System Restore checkpoint. Last resort before an in-place repair.
repairs.details: Creates a System Restore checkpoint FIRST (and aborts if it cannot), then runs the same scoped reset as wu-reset (including its managed-machine gating: on a WSUS-pinned, MDM-enrolled or domain-joined PC the WinHTTP proxy reset and the WSUS client-identity removal are skipped rather than executed, and the update-scan trigger checks its exit code and falls back to Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate.DetectNow()), and additionally resets the security descriptors of the wuauserv and bits services to the Microsoft-documented defaults with sc.exe sdset. This fixes the rare case where broken service ACLs (from malware cleanup or a bad tool) block the update stack. The CURRENT descriptors are captured with 'sc.exe sdshow' into the ledger before-state before they are overwritten, so they can be manually restored — WinUtil captures nothing. Still never touches Group Policy: no Policies hive deletion, no GroupPolicy folder removal, no secedit. A service in this set that is NOT PRESENT AT ALL fails the re-enable step rather than being noted in passing: these are core Windows client services, FrameForge cannot read or restore a start type for a service that does not exist, and a step that reports success for something it never measured is exactly what doctrine rule 2 forbids. The rest of the reset still runs; the run is simply reported as not completed.
whatItRuns: Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "%SystemDrive%\"

New-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force  (TEMPORARY: bypasses the once-per-24h throttle; the prior value — or its absence — is captured first)
Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'FrameForge: before <repair name>' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS

Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value <captured prior value>  — or Remove-ItemProperty when the value did not exist before. Runs in a finally block, so the throttle is put back even if Checkpoint-Computer fails.

Set-Service -StartupType <documented default> on any DISABLED service among: wuauserv=Manual, bits=Manual, cryptSvc=Automatic, msiserver=Manual, appidsvc=Manual, DoSvc=Automatic, UsoSvc=Automatic  (prior start type captured to the ledger; enabled services are left alone). Fallback when Set-Service is refused on a PROTECTED service (appidsvc is the usual one): Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>' -Name Start -Value <2=Automatic|3=Manual> -Type DWord
Get-BitsTransfer -AllUsers | Remove-BitsTransfer
Stop-Service -Name wuauserv, cryptSvc, bits, msiserver, appidsvc -Force
Move-Item %ALLUSERSPROFILE%\Microsoft\Network\Downloader\qmgr*.dat -> %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\backups\bits-queue-<timestamp>\  (moved, not deleted)
Rename-Item %SystemRoot%\SoftwareDistribution -> SoftwareDistribution.bak-<timestamp>
Rename-Item %SystemRoot%\System32\catroot2 -> catroot2.bak-<timestamp>

netsh winhttp reset proxy   (current setting captured via "netsh winhttp show proxy" in the ledger before-state; SKIPPED without running when this machine is WSUS-pinned, MDM-enrolled or domain-joined AND a proxy is actually configured — on a managed network clearing it cuts the machine off from updates rather than fixing them, and this repair is reversible:false so there would be no automatic way back)

Remove-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate' -Name AccountDomainSid, PingID, SusClientId, SusClientIdValidation  (prior values captured to the ledger; NOT run when HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate\WUServer pins this machine to a live WSUS server — removing a managed client's identity is an administrator action, not a user one)
sc.exe sdset wuauserv "D:(A;;CCLCSWRPWPDTLOCRRC;;;SY)(A;;CCDCLCSWRPWPDTLOCRSDRCWDWO;;;BA)(A;;CCLCSWLOCRRC;;;AU)(A;;CCLCSWRPWPDTLOCRRC;;;PU)"
