UsoClient.exe StartScan   (exit code checked, not discarded; when the verb is refused or missing on this build, (New-Object -ComObject Microsoft.Update.AutoUpdate).DetectNow() is used instead, and a scan that could not be triggered at all is reported as such)
repairs.risks: Overwrites the service ACLs of wuauserv and BITS with the documented defaults — a last resort. If an administrator had intentionally customized those ACLs, that customization is lost; the prior descriptors are recorded in the ledger (sdshow output) for manual restore via 'sc.exe sdset <service> <recorded SD>'. A System Restore checkpoint is created first and the repair refuses to run if it cannot be. Everything in the wu-reset risk note also applies, including its MANAGED MACHINES paragraph.
repairs.verifyAfter: Same as wu-reset: the windows-update probe is re-run; definitive confirmation is the next successful update scan. The restore point's sequence number is in the run result and the ledger — roll back with 'Restore-Computer -RestorePoint <n>' or rstrui.exe.

repairs.name: Repair the component store (DISM RestoreHealth, then SFC)
repairs.summary: Repairs the Windows component store with DISM, then runs SFC — in that order, because SFC repairs files FROM the store DISM just fixed.
repairs.details: Runs DISM /RestoreHealth (sourcing repair files from Windows Update by default), then chains sfc /scannow. The DISM-before-SFC ordering is the 2025-era consensus: SFC copies known-good files out of the component store (WinSxS), so a corrupt store must be repaired first — WinUtil runs SFC first and never re-runs it. When Windows Update itself is broken (error 0x800f081f), pass -SourcePath pointing at the install.wim or install.esd of a mounted ISO of the same build/edition; the engine then adds /Source:WIM|ESD:<path>:<index> /LimitAccess so DISM cannot fall back to broken WU. Append :<index> to the path to select an edition (defaults to 1). DISM is invoked with /English: its console output is MUI-localized, and both the success sentence quoted back to the user and the failure tail written to the ledger are English by construction, so without it they are dead text on a localized install. /English changes the output language only, never the operation or the exit code. The SFC pass that follows is graded ONLY from CBS.log [SR] lines written at or after that scan started — a 'Verify complete' left over from an earlier scan can no longer grade this one.
whatItRuns: Dism.exe /English /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth  [+ /Source:WIM:<path>:<index> /LimitAccess  or  /Source:ESD:<path>:<index> /LimitAccess  when -SourcePath is given]

sfc.exe /scannow   (outcome decided by exit code, then the [SR] markers written to %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log AT OR AFTER this scan started, then sfc's English console text — an outcome that none of those can establish is reported as indeterminate, never as success)
repairs.risks: Long-running (typically 10-30 minutes total). Replaces corrupt system files with canonical Microsoft-signed copies — there is no user state to restore, which is why no undo exists and why no restore point is created (System Restore does not snapshot WinSxS payloads in a way that would help here). Some repairs only complete at the next boot; a reboot afterwards is recommended. Without -SourcePath it downloads from Windows Update. Logs: %SystemRoot%\Logs\DISM\dism.log and %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log.
repairs.verifyAfter: The system-files probe is re-run (Repair-WindowsImage -CheckHealth corruption flag), and both tools' own result texts are parsed and reported verbatim. 'SFC found corrupt files but was unable to fix some of them' is reported as NOT fixed, with the advice to re-run with -SourcePath. The appended SFC step's outcome is established by exit code, then sfc's English console text, then the CBS.log [SR] markers; an outcome no rung can establish marks the run NOT completed rather than succeeded.

repairs.name: System File Checker (standalone)
repairs.summary: Scans all protected system files and repairs any that are corrupt, using the component store as the source.
repairs.details: Standalone sfc /scannow. Because SFC sources its repairs from the component store, prefer the dism-restorehealth repair (which runs DISM first, then SFC) when the store itself reports corruption — running SFC against a corrupt store repairs nothing. This standalone entry exists for the case where the store is healthy but SFC verification found violations. TIME SCOPING: the CBS.log [SR] lines are filtered to those written AT OR AFTER this scan started before anything is concluded from them. Without that filter a 'Verify complete' or a 'Cannot repair member file' from a scan weeks ago graded today's run — and on a localized Windows, where sfc's English console text never matches, the log is the deciding rung. If this scan left no attributable [SR] line, the outcome is reported as indeterminate, which counts as NOT completed.
whatItRuns: sfc.exe /scannow   (outcome decided by exit code, then the [SR] markers written to %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log AT OR AFTER this scan started, then sfc's English console text — an outcome that none of those can establish is reported as indeterminate, never as success)
repairs.risks: Takes 5-15 minutes. Replaces corrupt protected files with canonical copies from the component store; nothing user-specific is changed. Some repairs complete at the next boot. Detail log: %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log (lines tagged [SR]) — which is also where the engine reads the outcome from when sfc's own console text is localized.
repairs.verifyAfter: The outcome is established in three rungs, in order: sfc.exe's EXIT CODE; then sfc's own English console text ('did not find any integrity violations' / 'successfully repaired' / 'unable to fix'); then the [SR] markers in %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log ('Cannot repair member file' — unfixable, 'Repairing corrupted file' with no cannot-repair lines — repaired, 'Verify complete' with neither — clean), which the component store writes in English on every UI language. The CBS evidence lines are recorded in the run's mutations so the claim is auditable. If NO rung can decide, the result is reported as indeterminate and the run is marked NOT completed — sfc.exe exits 0 even when it reports files it could not repair, so treating an unread result as success would be claiming a repair that never happened. The system-files probe is then re-run.

repairs.name: Fix problems using Windows Update (guided in-place component reinstall)
repairs.summary: Opens Settings > System > Recovery so you can run "Fix problems using Windows Update" > Reinstall now: the same component replacement as an ISO in-place repair, from Windows Update, with one reboot and no ISO. The missing rung between DISM/SFC and the full in-place repair.
repairs.details: When dism-restorehealth and sfc-scannow cannot fix component corruption, the catalog used to jump straight to the full ISO in-place repair — 30-90 minutes, two or three reboots, a consent contract and BitLocker rails. Windows 11 23H2 (build 22631) added a much cheaper rung that does the same job: Settings > System > Recovery > "Fix problems using Windows Update" > Reinstall now re-downloads the CURRENT build's system files from Windows Update and replaces them in place, keeping files, apps and settings, with a single reboot and typically 20-40 minutes of work. FrameForge never mentioned it, so users on the builds where it exists were pushed up a far heavier rung than they needed. This is a GUIDED handoff, deliberately: the flow is a Settings UI action with no documented command line, so the engine opens the Recovery page and tells you exactly what to click. It does not script the click, and the run result does NOT claim the reinstall happened — it says only that the page was opened. Re-run the system-files probe after the reboot to confirm. The rung does not exist on Windows 11 21H2 (22000) or 22H2 (22621), so this entry carries minBuild 22631: on an older build it is still LISTED, with applicable:false and a reason naming the build, rather than hidden — a user who has read about the feature deserves to be told it is not on their build instead of wondering where it went.
whatItRuns: Start-Process ms-settings:recovery   (opens Settings > System > Recovery; the user clicks "Fix problems using Windows Update" > Reinstall now)
repairs.risks: FrameForge itself changes nothing here: it opens a Settings page. What YOU then start from that page is a real in-place component reinstall — it re-downloads several gigabytes from Windows Update, replaces the current build's system files, and reboots once. Files, apps and settings are kept, but like any in-place servicing operation it should not be interrupted, and a machine on a metered or slow connection will be busy for a while. It cannot be undone; the way back from a bad outcome is a System Restore point or a backup, which is why the heavier ISO in-place repair keeps its consent contract. On a build older than 22631 this repair refuses with errorCode 'not-applicable-on-this-build' instead of opening a page that has no such option.
repairs.verifyAfter: NOTHING is verified by the run itself, and the result says so: opening a Settings page is not a repair, and this step never reports the reinstall as done. After you complete the reinstall and the machine reboots, re-run the system-files probe (and dism-restorehealth's ScanHealth) to confirm the component store is healthy. The run's mutation record is a single 'guided-handoff' entry naming ms-settings:recovery, so the ledger cannot be mistaken for a record of a completed reinstall.

repairs.name: Scan the file system for errors (read-only)
repairs.summary: An online, read-only NTFS scan of the system drive — detects file-system damage without repairing anything and without locking the volume.
repairs.details: Runs Repair-Volume -Scan (the PowerShell form of 'chkdsk C: /scan'). Rung 0 of the repair ladder: file-system corruption undermines every repair above it, so when the disk probe reports NTFS/disk error events or a dirty bit, this runs first. It is online and read-only — the volume stays mounted, nothing is written, and the result ('NoErrorsFound' / 'ErrorsFound' / ...) decides whether chkdsk-spotfix or chkdsk-full-repair is warranted. Note what this repair honestly cannot do: it does not touch hardware findings. A failing drive (physical-disk-unhealthy) or an SSD near end of life (ssd-wear-critical) is a hardware problem no software repair fixes — the honest answer there is backup and replacement.
whatItRuns: Repair-Volume -DriveLetter <system drive> -Scan      (equivalent to "chkdsk C: /scan": online, read-only, no lock, never repairs)
repairs.risks: Effectively none: the scan is read-only and the volume stays online and usable. It does take minutes on a large volume and reads heavily from the drive. Marked not reversible only because there is nothing to reverse.
repairs.verifyAfter: The disk probe is re-run. The scan result itself is reported verbatim — 'NoErrorsFound' means the file system is clean and the disk events came from something else (usually the drive or its cable), which is a first-class result, not a failure to fix.

repairs.name: Spot-fix the file-system errors the scan found
repairs.summary: Fixes only the specific corruptions a prior scan queued — seconds to minutes, instead of the hours a full offline chkdsk takes.
repairs.details: Runs Repair-Volume -SpotFix ('chkdsk C: /spotfix'). Since Windows 8, NTFS self-healing queues detected corruptions and SpotFix repairs exactly those, so the volume is offline for seconds rather than hours. Detection uses the DEEP disk probe, whose online chkdsk scan is what queues the corruptions in the first place — detect (scan) then fix (spotfix) then verify (scan) is literally the same tool three times, which is the doctrine working as intended. On the volume Windows is running from, Windows normally defers the offline moment to the next restart; if the cmdlet reports the volume is in use, restart and re-run, or escalate to chkdsk-full-repair which schedules the offline pass explicitly.
whatItRuns: Repair-Volume -DriveLetter <system drive> -SpotFix   (equivalent to "chkdsk C: /spotfix": fixes only what the scan already flagged)
repairs.risks: File-system repair is inherently one-way: correcting a damaged directory entry or index can orphan the file it pointed at (orphans land in \found.000). System Restore does not snapshot NTFS metadata, so a checkpoint would be theatre here — the real protection is a backup, which matters most when the disk probe also reports media errors or drive wear. On the system volume the fix may be deferred to the next restart; the result says which happened.
repairs.verifyAfter: The deep disk probe is re-run: the dirty bit must be clear and an online scan must report NoErrorsFound. If the corruption was deferred to the next boot, the verify result says exactly that instead of claiming success.

repairs.name: Full offline disk check with bad-sector scan (next restart)
repairs.summary: Schedules chkdsk /f /r for the next restart: a full offline file-system repair plus a sector-by-sector surface scan. Hours, not minutes.
repairs.details: Runs 'chkdsk <system drive> /f /r' and answers Y to its scheduling prompt. The volume Windows runs from can never be checked offline while Windows is running, so this ALWAYS schedules for the next restart — the check then runs before Windows starts. /f repairs the file system; /r additionally reads every sector, relocating data away from bad ones. This is the last software rung for disk problems and it is the slow one: hours on a large spinning drive, and it should not be interrupted. Cancel a scheduled check with 'chkntfs /x <drive>'. A System Restore checkpoint is created first (aggressive tier) even though System Restore cannot undo file-system repairs — it protects the rest of the machine state around a rung this heavy.
whatItRuns: Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "%SystemDrive%\"

New-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force  (TEMPORARY: bypasses the once-per-24h throttle; the prior value — or its absence — is captured first)
Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'FrameForge: before <repair name>' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS

Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value <captured prior value>  — or Remove-ItemProperty when the value did not exist before. Runs in a finally block, so the throttle is put back even if Checkpoint-Computer fails.

chkdsk.exe <system drive> /f /r   (answering Y to "schedule this volume to be checked the next time the system restarts?" — the system volume can never be checked while Windows is running. Whether the check was actually scheduled is then read STRUCTURALLY from HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\BootExecute and the volume dirty bit, not from chkdsk's output text)
repairs.risks: IRREVERSIBLE and SLOW. The check runs before Windows boots and can take several hours with /r on a large drive; the PC is unusable for that whole time and interrupting an offline chkdsk mid-write can itself cause damage. Repairs can orphan files into \found.000. On a drive that is already failing (media errors, unhealthy status), the sustained full-surface read of /r can be the load that finishes it off — back up first. Cancel a scheduled check before restarting with 'chkntfs /x <drive>'.
repairs.verifyAfter: Nothing is verifiable until after the restart: the run result says only whether the check was SCHEDULED, never that the disk was repaired. Whether it was scheduled is read structurally — HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\BootExecute is captured before the command and re-read after, and a new autocheck entry naming this volume is the proof (the default 'autocheck autochk *' entry means nothing on its own); the volume dirty bit corroborates it. Only when BOTH of those reads succeed and both say no is it reported that nothing was scheduled; when neither can be read the step reports honestly that it could not confirm either way and points at 'chkntfs <drive>', rather than asserting that nothing will happen at the next boot. After the restart the deep disk probe is re-run (dirty bit, online scan, drive health) and the boot-time chkdsk result is in the Application log under source 'Chkdsk' / 'Wininit' (event 1001).

repairs.name: Flush DNS and renew the DHCP lease (gentle tier)
repairs.summary: Clears the DNS resolver cache and requests a fresh IP configuration — the gentle network fix to try before any stack reset.
repairs.details: ipconfig /flushdns clears stale or poisoned DNS cache entries (the canonical fix when the health probe shows the 'internet works by raw IP but names do not resolve' pattern). /release + /renew drops and re-requests the DHCP lease, fixing stale IP/gateway/DNS assignments. Current adapter configuration (IP, gateway, DNS servers per adapter) is captured to the ledger first.
whatItRuns: ipconfig /flushdns
ipconfig /release
ipconfig /renew
repairs.risks: Connectivity drops for a few seconds during release/renew. Adapters with static IP configuration are unaffected by release/renew (ipconfig reports them and moves on). The flushed DNS cache cannot be un-flushed, which is why this is marked not reversible; it simply refills with use.
repairs.verifyAfter: The network probe is re-run: link, gateway, raw-IP internet, DNS resolution, and the NCSI HTTP endpoint are each tested again.

repairs.name: Switch to a different DNS resolver
repairs.summary: Points every connected adapter at a known-good public resolver (Cloudflare by default) — the targeted fix when the internet works by raw IP but names do not resolve.
repairs.details: The network probe's discriminator is the whole point of this repair: if 1.1.1.1 answers but microsoft.com does not resolve, the problem is the resolver, not connectivity, and flushing or resetting the stack fixes nothing. This sets the DNS servers on every connected physical adapter to a chosen provider and flushes the cache. Providers (WinUtil's config/dns.json set): cloudflare (1.1.1.1 / 1.0.0.1), google (8.8.8.8 / 8.8.4.4), quad9 (9.9.9.9 / 149.112.112.112), adguard, opendns, and 'dhcp' to go back to automatic. Choose with -DnsProvider <key>. IPv6 servers are set only on adapters that actually have IPv6 bound. Fully reversible: the prior per-adapter servers — and whether they were DHCP-assigned rather than manually set, which is a distinction a naive undo gets wrong — are captured to the ledger, and undo restores exactly that.
whatItRuns: Set-DnsClientServerAddress -InterfaceIndex <each connected physical adapter> -ServerAddresses 1.1.1.1, 1.0.0.1  [+ 2606:4700:4700::1111, 2606:4700:4700::1001 on adapters with IPv6 bound]   (-DnsProvider cloudflare = Cloudflare)
ipconfig /flushdns
repairs.risks: Changes which company resolves your domain names, which is a privacy choice as much as a technical one — every site name you visit is sent to that provider. On a corporate or home network with a local DNS server, an external resolver breaks name resolution for internal hostnames (printers, NAS, intranet); use -DnsProvider dhcp to go back. Filtering resolvers (Quad9, AdGuard) deliberately block some domains. Undo restores the captured per-adapter configuration exactly, including 'it was DHCP-assigned'.
repairs.verifyAfter: The network probe is re-run: name resolution must succeed while raw-IP reachability stays working. If DNS still fails against a known-good public resolver, the problem is upstream filtering or a captive portal, and the verify result says so rather than claiming a fix.

repairs.name: Reset Winsock and the TCP/IP stack
repairs.summary: Resets the Winsock catalog and the IP stack to install defaults — the escalation when flushing, renewing, and changing resolver did not help.
repairs.details: netsh winsock reset rebuilds the Winsock catalog, removing broken Layered Service Providers left behind by VPNs, firewalls, or malware. netsh int ip reset rewrites the TCP/IP stack registry keys to defaults; it is given an explicit log path (%LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\logs\ip-reset-<timestamp>.log) because it normally exits NON-ZERO — 'access denied' on a handful of ACL-protected subkeys is the expected benign result — and whether it did the work is judged by the exit code plus whether that log was actually written, never by matching English words in its output. Requires a reboot to fully take effect. Because the effect is a broad rewrite of networking registry state that the ledger cannot faithfully restore, a System Restore checkpoint is enforced first even though this is a standard-tier repair. Note WinUtil's standalone network fix is only these two commands; FrameForge offers the gentler network-flush and dns-change-resolver first, and captures the current adapter configuration before resetting.
whatItRuns: Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "%SystemDrive%\"

New-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force  (TEMPORARY: bypasses the once-per-24h throttle; the prior value — or its absence — is captured first)
Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'FrameForge: before <repair name>' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS

Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value <captured prior value>  — or Remove-ItemProperty when the value did not exist before. Runs in a finally block, so the throttle is put back even if Checkpoint-Computer fails.
netsh winsock reset

netsh int ip reset "%LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\logs\ip-reset-<timestamp>.log"   (an explicit log path, so a non-zero exit can be judged by whether netsh actually wrote a reset log instead of by matching English words in its output)
repairs.risks: Third-party LSPs (some VPN/firewall/antivirus network filters) are removed from the catalog and those products may need a repair/reinstall. Custom TCP/IP settings (static IPs, custom metrics, custom DNS) can be reset to defaults — the ledger records each adapter's IP, gateway, and DNS servers beforehand so they can be re-entered manually, and a System Restore checkpoint is created first. A reboot is required before judging the result.
repairs.verifyAfter: The network probe is re-run immediately, with the honest caveat that the reset only fully applies after the reboot. A non-zero exit from 'netsh int ip reset' accompanied by a written reset log is reported as APPLIED WITH BENIGN WARNINGS (reboot required), not as a failure; only a non-zero exit with no log is a genuine failure. The exit code and the log path are recorded in the run's mutations either way.

repairs.name: Reset the Microsoft Store cache
repairs.summary: Runs WSReset to clear the Store's local cache without changing account settings or installed apps.
repairs.details: WSReset.exe clears the Microsoft Store cache — the first-line fix for a Store that opens to a blank page, spins forever, or fails downloads with cache-related errors. It does not touch installed apps, licenses, or account settings. It deliberately does NOT claim to address the store-service-disabled finding: clearing a cache cannot re-enable a disabled service, and pretending otherwise is exactly the kind of false promise this catalog exists to avoid. That finding belongs to store-services-enable.
whatItRuns: WSReset.exe  (started hidden, waited on for up to 120 s)
repairs.risks: The Store app may open by itself when WSReset finishes — that is WSReset's built-in behavior, not an error. The cleared cache is not recoverable (it rebuilds automatically on next use).
repairs.verifyAfter: The store probe is re-run: package status, dependency services, and recent deployment errors.

repairs.name: Re-enable the Microsoft Store's dependency services
repairs.summary: Restores the documented start type of any disabled Store dependency service (AppX Deployment, Client Licensing, Install Service, Delivery Optimization) and starts it.
repairs.details: The Store cannot install, license, or update anything while its dependency services are Disabled — a state 'debloat' scripts and service-tuning guides leave behind routinely, and one that no cache reset or re-registration can recover from. This restores AppXSvc=Manual, ClipSVC=Manual, InstallService=Manual, DoSvc=Automatic, but ONLY for services detection actually found Disabled: a service an administrator deliberately set to Manual or Automatic is left exactly as it is. The prior start type of every service is captured to the ledger before the change. AppXSvc and ClipSVC are demand-started, so a direct Start-Service can be refused — that is normal and reported honestly; the restored start type is what matters.
whatItRuns: Set-Service -StartupType <documented default> on any DISABLED service among: AppXSvc=Manual, ClipSVC=Manual, InstallService=Manual, DoSvc=Automatic  (prior start type captured to the ledger; enabled services are left alone). Fallback when Set-Service is refused on a PROTECTED service (appidsvc is the usual one): Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>' -Name Start -Value <2=Automatic|3=Manual> -Type DWord
Start-Service on each service this run re-enabled from Disabled
repairs.risks: Re-enabling these services undoes a deliberate 'debloat' choice if one was made — Delivery Optimization in particular is disabled by some users to stop peer-to-peer update sharing (its bandwidth behaviour is configurable separately). Only services found Disabled are touched. Marked not reversible because undo is a one-liner the run result spells out: Set-Service -Name <name> -StartupType Disabled, with the prior state recorded in the ledger.
repairs.verifyAfter: The store probe is re-run: no dependency service may report Disabled, and the Store package status is re-read.

repairs.name: Re-register the Microsoft Store app
repairs.summary: Re-registers the Store package for the current user from its own manifest — fixes a Store whose package status is not Ok.
repairs.details: Runs Add-AppxPackage -Register against the installed Store package's AppxManifest.xml with -DisableDevelopmentMode, which re-registers the app from its already-present files (nothing is downloaded). This is the canonical fix when the health probe shows the Store package status as something other than 'Ok'.
whatItRuns: Get-AppxPackage -Name Microsoft.WindowsStore | ForEach-Object { Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -Register "$($_.InstallLocation)\AppxManifest.xml" }
repairs.risks: Minimal: re-registration re-reads the existing manifest; installed apps, licenses, and settings are untouched. If the Store package files themselves are missing this fails with a clear error (the fix for that is store-reregister-all or a Windows repair).
repairs.verifyAfter: The store probe is re-run; the Store package should report status 'Ok'.

repairs.name: Re-register every Store app for all users (aggressive)
repairs.summary: The nuclear Appx re-register: every installed package, all users, behind an enforced System Restore checkpoint. Only for when the single-package re-register did not help.
repairs.details: Enumerates every Appx package for all users and re-registers each from its manifest. Errors on protected/staged system packages are expected and counted honestly rather than hidden — a handful of failures among hundreds of successes is normal and harmless. A System Restore checkpoint is created first because this touches the registration state of every packaged app on the machine, including shell surfaces. WHAT DECIDES THE RESULT: the bulk count does NOT. After the pass the engine looks up Microsoft.WindowsStore by name for the current user, and it is that named check (the same read-only shape the store health probe uses) that decides the step. A run that re-registers hundreds of packages but leaves the Store unregistered is reported as NOT completed, because a total is not evidence about the one package this repair claims the store-missing / store-package-broken findings for. If the Store cannot be re-registered here it is almost certainly deprovisioned or absent from the image, which re-registration cannot recover — the next rung is a repair install (image.ps1).
whatItRuns: Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "%SystemDrive%\"

New-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force  (TEMPORARY: bypasses the once-per-24h throttle; the prior value — or its absence — is captured first)
Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'FrameForge: before <repair name>' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS

Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value <captured prior value>  — or Remove-ItemProperty when the value did not exist before. Runs in a finally block, so the throttle is put back even if Checkpoint-Computer fails.
Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers | ForEach-Object { Add-AppxPackage -DisableDevelopmentMode -Register "$($_.InstallLocation)\AppxManifest.xml" }  (each package individually try/caught)
repairs.risks: Takes several minutes. Protected system packages fail to re-register by design (reported, ignorable). Start menu and shell apps may briefly restart as their packages re-register. No user data or app settings are removed. A System Restore checkpoint is created first and the repair refuses to run if it cannot be.
repairs.verifyAfter: The store probe is re-run: package status, dependency services, deployment errors.

repairs.name: Rebuild the Windows Search index
repairs.summary: Re-enables Windows Search if it was disabled, stops the indexer, sets the old index database aside (renamed, not deleted), flags a rebuild, and restarts — search re-indexes from scratch.
repairs.details: If WSearch is Disabled (a state health.ps1 reports as wsearch-disabled and which Start-Service cannot recover from), its start type is restored to Automatic first — otherwise the final start step fails and the rebuild never begins. Then: stops WSearch, renames the index database (Windows.edb, or Windows.db on newer builds) to a timestamped .bak name, sets HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Search\SetupCompletedSuccessfully=0 (the same switch as Settings > Searching Windows > Advanced > Rebuild), and restarts WSearch, which rebuilds the index from scratch. The prior service start type, the prior value of the registry switch, and the old database's name and size are all captured to the ledger. If WSearch is not present on this system at all, the enable step FAILS rather than reporting that there was nothing to do: a start type that was never read cannot be restored, and the rebuild that follows would be meaningless.
whatItRuns: Set-Service -StartupType <documented default> on any DISABLED service among: WSearch=Automatic  (prior start type captured to the ledger; enabled services are left alone). Fallback when Set-Service is refused on a PROTECTED service (appidsvc is the usual one): Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>' -Name Start -Value <2=Automatic|3=Manual> -Type DWord
Stop-Service -Name WSearch -Force
Rename-Item %ProgramData%\Microsoft\Search\Data\Applications\Windows\Windows.edb -> Windows.edb.bak-<timestamp>  (retried while the indexer releases its lock)
Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Search' -Name SetupCompletedSuccessfully -Value 0
Start-Service -Name WSearch
repairs.risks: Search results are incomplete for hours while the index rebuilds (longer on large drives). The old index file is renamed, not deleted — its .bak name is in the ledger and it can be deleted later to reclaim space (often multiple GB). CPU/disk activity from SearchIndexer is elevated during the rebuild. If WSearch had been deliberately disabled, this re-enables it (recorded in the ledger; set it back with Set-Service -Name WSearch -StartupType Disabled).
repairs.verifyAfter: The search probe is re-run: WSearch running, indexer process alive, and a fresh (small, growing) index file present. A freshly-started rebuild is reported as such, not claimed as instantly complete.

repairs.name: Restart the shell (Start menu, search UI, Explorer)
repairs.summary: Restarts StartMenuExperienceHost, SearchHost, and Explorer — instant, self-healing, fixes a hung Start menu or search pane.
repairs.details: Kills the two shell UI hosts and Explorer. All three are self-healing: Windows relaunches the hosts on demand and the engine relaunches Explorer immediately if Windows does not. Open Explorer windows close; running apps are unaffected. This is the 'have you turned the shell off and on again' fix and is completely safe. Note what is NOT in relevantFindings: health.ps1 emits startmenu-host-not-running at severity 'info' (StartMenuExperienceHost is demand-started, so it being absent is normal), and the engine ignores info-severity findings when deciding whether a repair applies. Listing it here would have been a pattern that could never match — a promise in the catalog that no run could ever keep — so it was removed rather than quietly left in.
whatItRuns: Stop-Process -Name StartMenuExperienceHost, SearchHost -Force  (if running)
Stop-Process -Name explorer -Force
Start-Process explorer.exe  (only if Windows has not already relaunched it)
repairs.risks: Open File Explorer windows close and the taskbar disappears for a second or two. No data or settings are touched. Undo is a no-op by nature: the restarted processes are stateless and relaunch automatically.
repairs.verifyAfter: After a short settle delay: Explorer is confirmed running and the search probe is re-run.

repairs.name: Clear the print spooler queue
repairs.summary: Stops the spooler, moves stuck spool files to a backup folder (not deleted), and restarts — the canonical fix for a jammed print queue.
repairs.details: Stops the Spooler service, MOVES everything in System32\spool\PRINTERS to %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\backups\spool-<timestamp>\ (WinUtil deletes these files; FrameForge moves them so nothing is unrecoverable), then restarts the Spooler. The moved file names are recorded in the ledger. Note what is deliberately absent: health.ps1 reports a DISABLED spooler as severity 'info', not a fault, because disabling the print spooler is a common and legitimate choice on a gaming rig (and a standard PrintNightmare mitigation). This repair therefore does not re-enable it — it would be overriding a deliberate decision, not fixing a fault. Honest about its own reach, too: printer-error-state is in relevantFindings because a jammed queue is a common cause of a printer sitting in Error, but a printer reported Offline is usually off, asleep, or off the network, and clearing the spool folder cannot do a thing about that. Every step can succeed while the printer stays offline — which is why a run reports stepsCompleted and verified separately, and only 'addressed' (both) means the finding is gone. See resultFieldsNote.
whatItRuns: Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force
Move-Item %SystemRoot%\System32\spool\PRINTERS\* -> %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state\backups\spool-<timestamp>\  (moved, not deleted)
Start-Service -Name Spooler
repairs.risks: All pending print jobs are cancelled and must be printed again. The raw spool files are preserved in the backup folder (path in the ledger) but re-submitting them as jobs is not generally possible — which is why this is marked not reversible despite nothing being deleted.
repairs.verifyAfter: The printing probe is re-run: spooler running, spool folder empty, no jobs stuck in Error/Blocked.

repairs.name: Restart the audio services
repairs.summary: Restarts AudioEndpointBuilder and then Audiosrv, in that order — the canonical fix for audio that stopped working after sleep or a driver hiccup.
repairs.details: Order matters: Audiosrv depends on AudioEndpointBuilder, so the endpoint builder is restarted first (its dependents restart with it), then Audiosrv is confirmed running. Service states and start types are captured to the ledger before the restart, and undo restores the captured run-states.
whatItRuns: Restart-Service -Name AudioEndpointBuilder -Force  (Audiosrv restarts with it as a dependent)
Start-Service -Name Audiosrv  (if it did not come back on its own)
repairs.risks: Audio cuts out for a few seconds during the restart; apps holding an audio stream may need the output device re-selected. Nothing persistent changes.
repairs.verifyAfter: The audio probe is re-run: both services running and no device in an error state.

repairs.name: Fix time synchronization (NTP)
repairs.summary: Points the Windows Time service at pool.ntp.org and forces a resync — fixes TLS/store/update failures caused by a wrong clock.
repairs.details: Captures the current time configuration — the peer list and sync type read straight from HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\Parameters (NtpServer, Type), where Windows stores them verbatim and UNLOCALIZED — to the ledger, then configures pool.ntp.org as the manual peer, restarts the time service, and forces a resync. Detection is a local read-only check (health.ps1 has no time category): the W32Time service state plus whether the System event log carries a successful time-sync event (Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service id 35) inside the last 7 days — a numeric event id, not a localized label. If the log does not reach back that far, detection says it could not determine rather than guessing. DOMAIN MEMBERS ARE REFUSED: a machine joined to a domain takes its clock from the domain hierarchy (Type NT5DS), and repointing it at pool.ntp.org risks Kerberos logon, share and authentication failures once the clock drifts past the five-minute tolerance — so detection returns 'not-applicable' with that explanation and the fix does not run. If you override it with -Force, the fix step still refuses to rewrite the peer list on a domain member: it runs 'w32tm /config /syncfromflags:DOMHIER /update' instead, which resyncs from the hierarchy. Fully reversible — undo restores the captured peer list, or domain-hierarchy sync when the captured Type was NT5DS, and REFUSES outright (rather than applying an assumed time.windows.com default) if the prior configuration was never captured.
whatItRuns: Start-Service -Name w32time  (if stopped)

w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:"pool.ntp.org,0x8" /syncfromflags:MANUAL /update   — EXCEPT on a domain-joined machine whose W32Time Type is NT5DS (or cannot be read), where this becomes "w32tm /config /syncfromflags:DOMHIER /update": a domain member must keep taking its clock from the domain hierarchy, because repointing it at pool.ntp.org risks Kerberos logon failures once the clock drifts past the five-minute tolerance
Restart-Service -Name w32time
w32tm /resync
repairs.risks: On an unmanaged machine the configured NTP peer changes to pool.ntp.org; the prior peer list and Type are captured from the registry and restored by undo. On a DOMAIN-JOINED machine this repair refuses by default and, even under -Force, never repoints the peer list — it re-applies domain-hierarchy sync (/syncfromflags:DOMHIER) instead, so domain time is not broken. Undo will not guess: if the prior configuration was not captured it refuses and tells you the exact command to run by hand. The system clock may step visibly if it was far off.
repairs.verifyAfter: The same local probe is re-run: the W32Time service must be running and the System event log must show a successful time-sync event (Microsoft-Windows-Time-Service id 35) inside the staleness window. Event ids are numeric and identical on every UI language, so the verification works on localized Windows — and when the log cannot answer, the result says 'could not determine' instead of claiming success.

repairs.name: Clean temporary files
repairs.summary: Deletes files from the user and system temp folders, skipping anything in use, and reports exactly how many files and bytes were removed.
repairs.details: Deletes files under %TEMP% and %SystemRoot%\Temp (system temp only when elevated; when run unelevated the system temp is skipped and the report says so). Every file is deleted individually inside try/catch: files locked by running programs are skipped and counted, never forced. Subdirectories left empty afterwards are removed on a best-effort basis as part of the same step. The honest per-folder tally (deleted count, deleted bytes, skipped count) goes into the result and the ledger — no inflated 'GB freed' claims.
whatItRuns: Get-ChildItem %TEMP% -Recurse -Force -File | Remove-Item  (each file individually; in-use files skipped)
Get-ChildItem %SystemRoot%\Temp -Recurse -Force -File | Remove-Item  (elevated only; same per-file handling)
repairs.risks: Deleted temp files are gone (not recycled). Rarely, a badly-written installer keeps needed state in temp — if an install is mid-flight, finish it first. Files in use are automatically skipped, so a running app cannot lose its working files.
repairs.verifyAfter: The disk-space probe is re-run and the result reports the exact deleted/skipped tallies per folder.

repairs.name: Component store cleanup (safe tier)
repairs.summary: DISM StartComponentCleanup: reclaims superseded component-store space WITHOUT /ResetBase, so existing updates stay uninstallable.
repairs.details: Runs the safe component-store cleanup that removes superseded component versions. Deliberately does NOT pass /ResetBase (WinUtil's Disk Cleanup tweak always does): /ResetBase additionally makes every installed update permanent and un-uninstallable, which belongs behind an explicit aggressive-tier choice (component-cleanup-resetbase). Detection uses the deep disk-space probe, which parses DISM AnalyzeComponentStore's 'Component Store Cleanup Recommended' verdict. The command is run with /English so the output recorded in the ledger, and any failure tail a user is asked to read back, are in the language this catalog describes. /English changes the output language only — never the operation, and never the exit code, which is what decides the verdict.
whatItRuns: Dism.exe /English /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
repairs.risks: Takes several minutes to an hour. Removed superseded components cannot be restored (that is the point), but installed updates remain uninstallable normally. Safe to interrupt-resistant: DISM handles interruption, but let it finish.
repairs.verifyAfter: The deep disk-space probe is re-run; DISM AnalyzeComponentStore should no longer recommend cleanup.

repairs.name: Component store cleanup with /ResetBase (aggressive)
repairs.summary: Maximum component-store space reclaim — at the permanent cost that no currently installed update can ever be uninstalled again. Behind an enforced System Restore checkpoint.
repairs.details: StartComponentCleanup with /ResetBase removes ALL superseded versions of every component. The extra space over the safe tier comes with a permanent, documented trade: every update installed so far becomes part of the base and can no longer be uninstalled. This is irreversible by design, which is why it sits behind the aggressive tier and an enforced System Restore checkpoint instead of being silently bundled into a 'disk cleanup' button. The command is run with /English so the output recorded in the ledger, and any failure tail a user is asked to read back, are in the language this catalog describes. /English changes the output language only — never the operation, and never the exit code, which is what decides the verdict.
whatItRuns: Enable-ComputerRestore -Drive "%SystemDrive%\"

New-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value 0 -PropertyType DWord -Force  (TEMPORARY: bypasses the once-per-24h throttle; the prior value — or its absence — is captured first)
Checkpoint-Computer -Description 'FrameForge: before <repair name>' -RestorePointType MODIFY_SETTINGS

Set-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SystemRestore' -Name SystemRestorePointCreationFrequency -Value <captured prior value>  — or Remove-ItemProperty when the value did not exist before. Runs in a finally block, so the throttle is put back even if Checkpoint-Computer fails.
Dism.exe /English /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup /ResetBase
repairs.risks: IRREVERSIBLE: after /ResetBase, no currently installed update can be uninstalled, ever — if the latest cumulative update has a regression, rolling it back is no longer possible. A System Restore checkpoint is created first and the repair refuses to run if it cannot be, but be honest about what that checkpoint does and does not cover: it restores registry and system state, it does not put superseded WinSxS payloads back. Only run when disk space matters more than update rollback. Takes several minutes to an hour.
repairs.verifyAfter: The deep disk-space probe is re-run; AnalyzeComponentStore should report no cleanup recommended and a smaller store.

repairs.name: Retry Windows activation
repairs.summary: Forces an online activation attempt against Microsoft's activation servers and reports the real error code when it fails.
repairs.details: Runs slmgr /ato, the documented way to force an activation attempt for a licence that is present but not in the Licensed state (grace period, notification state, or a transient server failure). Detection is the activation health probe reading LicenseStatus straight from the Software Licensing service, so this repair refuses outright on an already-activated machine. Whether it SUCCEEDED is not read from slmgr's output, which is fully localized — it is re-read from SoftwareLicensingProduct.LicenseStatus, the same structured source the health probe and the state capture use, so fix and verify are judged by identical evidence. When activation fails, the raw error is surfaced with its meaning rather than a generic 'something went wrong' (hex result codes are not localized, so this works everywhere): 0xC004F213 means no key or digital licence is present for this device, 0xC004C003 means the server refused the key (typically after a hardware change, where the fix is Settings > Activation > Troubleshoot with the Microsoft account that holds the digital licence). FrameForge never enters, generates, or alters a product key. CHANNEL GATE: every Windows licence row carrying a partial product key is enumerated (not an arbitrary first row out of an unordered CIM result), and the channel is read structurally from ProductKeyChannel, falling back to the invariant channel token inside Description and then to 'unknown'. On a VOLUME/KMS client (Volume:GVLK) or a SUBSCRIPTION licence this repair REFUSES as not-applicable: a KMS client activates against a KMS host on the local network rather than Microsoft, and subscription activation comes from the signed-in user's entitlement in Entra ID — in both cases slmgr /ato cannot fix what is actually broken, and the summary above would stop being a true description of what runs. -Force overrides deliberately.
whatItRuns: cscript.exe //nologo %SystemRoot%\System32\slmgr.vbs /ato   (force an online activation attempt against Microsoft's activation servers; the RESULT is then read from SoftwareLicensingProduct.LicenseStatus — the same structured source the health probe and the state capture use — not from slmgr's localized output)
repairs.risks: Contacts Microsoft's activation servers over the internet with this device's existing licence information. It does not change, install, or remove a product key, and it cannot deactivate a working licence. On a machine with no licence at all it simply fails with 0xC004F213 and says so.
repairs.verifyAfter: The activation probe is re-run: LicenseStatus must read 1 (Licensed). The fix step itself already re-queries the same SoftwareLicensingProduct property immediately after slmgr /ato rather than looking for the word 'successfully' in localized output, so a successful activation on a non-English machine is reported as success. Anything else is reported as not fixed, with the licensing error code and what it actually means; if the licensing service cannot be queried at all the step says it could not determine, instead of guessing either way.

repairs.name: Repair the WinGet package manager
repairs.summary: Reinstalls/repairs the App Installer (WinGet) via the Microsoft.WinGet.Client PowerShell module — the modern fix for a missing or broken winget.
repairs.details: Detection is a local read-only check: is winget on PATH and does 'winget --version' succeed (health.ps1 has no category for this). Before bootstrapping anything the engine checks two things that make this repair impossible on a hardened fleet and names the cause instead of surfacing a raw PowerShellGet exception: whether PowerShell is in FullLanguage mode (WDAC/AppLocker enforcement drops it to ConstrainedLanguage, where Install-Module and the provider bootstrap simply cannot run) and whether the PowerShell Gallery is reachable (corporate proxies routinely block it). The fix then bootstraps the NuGet provider and the Microsoft.WinGet.Client module if the Repair-WinGetPackageManager cmdlet is not already available, then runs Repair-WinGetPackageManager -AllUsers -Latest — the same modern path WinUtil uses, with the bootstrap steps skipped when already present instead of always reinstalling.
whatItRuns: Read $ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode, then Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://www.powershellgallery.com/api/v2" -UseBasicParsing -TimeoutSec 10   (read-only preflight: WDAC/AppLocker ConstrainedLanguage or a blocked gallery is named as the cause instead of surfacing a raw PowerShellGet exception)
Install-PackageProvider -Name NuGet -Force  (only if Repair-WinGetPackageManager is not already available)

Install-Module -Name Microsoft.WinGet.Client -Force  (only if not already available; installs machine-wide under %ProgramFiles%\WindowsPowerShell\Modules, and the install is recorded in the run's mutations because this repair is reversible:false and the module is left behind)
Repair-WinGetPackageManager -AllUsers -Latest
repairs.risks: Installs the Microsoft.WinGet.Client PowerShell module from the PowerShell Gallery and downloads the latest App Installer package from Microsoft — both are network operations from Microsoft-controlled sources. Installed winget packages and their sources are untouched. The Microsoft.WinGet.Client module is installed MACHINE-WIDE under %ProgramFiles%\WindowsPowerShell\Modules and, because this repair is reversible:false, it is left behind: the install is recorded in the run's mutations with its path, the ledger before-state records whether the module was already present, and you can remove it with 'Uninstall-Module -Name Microsoft.WinGet.Client -AllVersions'. On a machine in ConstrainedLanguage mode or without access to the PowerShell Gallery the repair stops at the first step with a message naming that cause, rather than failing obscurely.
repairs.verifyAfter: The local winget check is re-run: winget must be on PATH and 'winget --version' must succeed.

repairs.name: Enable .NET Framework 3.5 (covers 2.0 and 3.0)
repairs.summary: Turns on the NetFx3 Windows optional feature — the fix for an application that refuses to start saying it needs .NET Framework 3.5.
repairs.details: Detection is a local read-only check: Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3 reports the feature's real State (health.ps1 has no category for optional features). If it is already Enabled the repair REFUSES with the first-class 'nothing to do here' result. If it is Disabled the engine does NOT claim to have found a fault — a disabled NetFx3 is the Windows default on every clean install, and detection says exactly that: it reports the real state, reports reason 'user-initiated', and enables the feature on request without pretending it diagnosed a problem. Only you know whether an application needs it. The fix is one documented call, Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3 -All -NoRestart, and -All pulls in the child features (WCF HTTP/non-HTTP activation) that the parent alone leaves off.
whatItRuns: Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3 -All -NoRestart   (payload comes from Windows Update on demand, so this needs working internet; pass -SourcePath <mounted media>\sources\sxs to install offline instead)
repairs.risks: Adds the .NET Framework 3.5 runtime to Windows. Nothing existing is changed, removed, or reconfigured, and no other feature is touched. .NET 3.5 is a Feature on Demand: its payload is NOT on the disk of a normal Windows 11 install, so enabling it downloads from Windows Update and therefore needs working internet — on a machine with no route to Windows Update (or a WSUS policy that blocks Features on Demand) it fails with 0x800F0906 or 0x800F081F and says so. Mount matching Windows installation media and pass -SourcePath <drive>:\sources\sxs to install it offline instead (the engine then adds -LimitAccess so it cannot silently fall back to Windows Update). The feature's exact prior State is captured before anything changes, and undo restores that captured state rather than an assumed default.
repairs.verifyAfter: The same read-only DISM query is re-run: Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3 must report Enabled. EnablePending (enabled, restart outstanding) is reported honestly as needing a restart rather than claimed as complete.

repairs.name: Enable .NET Framework 4.x advanced services (WCF activation)
repairs.featurePurpose: the .NET Framework 4.x advanced services (ASP.NET 4.x and WCF HTTP/TCP/named-pipe activation)
repairs.summary: Turns on the NetFx4-AdvSrvs optional feature and its children — needed by applications and local services that use WCF activation or ASP.NET 4.x.
repairs.details: NetFx4-AdvSrvs is enabled on a stock Windows 11, so finding it Disabled usually means it was turned off deliberately or by a hardening script, and an application that depends on WCF activation then fails at startup. Detection reads the real State with Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online and refuses when it is already Enabled. When it is Disabled the engine reports that state as-is under reason 'user-initiated' rather than calling it a fault, because a disabled optional feature is a configuration, not a detected defect. -All is passed so the child features (WCF-HTTP-Activation45, WCF-TCP-Activation45, WCF-Pipe-Activation45, ASPNET45) come with it — enabling the parent alone leaves them off and the application still fails.
whatItRuns: Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx4-AdvSrvs -All -NoRestart   (payload comes from Windows Update on demand, so this needs working internet; pass -SourcePath <mounted media>\sources\sxs to install offline instead)
repairs.risks: Adds .NET 4.x advanced services and their child activation components to Windows. Nothing existing is changed or removed. Unlike .NET 3.5 the payload for this one normally IS on disk, so it usually installs without any network access; if it has been removed from the image the same Feature-on-Demand rules apply and -SourcePath <drive>:\sources\sxs makes it an offline install. The exact prior State is captured and undo restores it.
repairs.verifyAfter: Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx4-AdvSrvs is re-run and must report Enabled; EnablePending is reported as 'needs a restart', not as done.

repairs.name: Enable DirectPlay (legacy game compatibility)
repairs.featurePurpose: the legacy DirectPlay networking runtime that pre-2010 games call at startup
repairs.summary: Turns on the DirectPlay legacy component — the fix for an older game that closes immediately or errors about dplayx.dll on launch.
repairs.details: DirectPlay is the retired DirectX networking layer. It is off by default on Windows 10/11, and a lot of games from roughly 1998-2010 still call it and simply exit when it is missing. Detection reads the feature's real State with Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online and refuses if it is already Enabled. If it is Disabled the engine reports exactly that under reason 'user-initiated': off is the Windows default, not a fault, and whether you need it depends on the game you are trying to run — FrameForge will not dress a default up as a detected problem. -All is passed so the LegacyComponents parent is enabled along with it, which is required for DirectPlay to actually turn on.
whatItRuns: Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName DirectPlay -All -NoRestart   (payload comes from Windows Update on demand, so this needs working internet; pass -SourcePath <mounted media>\sources\sxs to install offline instead)
repairs.risks: Adds a deprecated but Microsoft-shipped DirectX component. It is not a security fix and not a performance change — it will not make any modern game faster, and nothing in FrameForge will claim it did. Enabling it also enables its LegacyComponents parent. Payload usually comes from Windows Update on demand, so it can need internet; -SourcePath <drive>:\sources\sxs installs it from mounted media instead. The prior State of the feature is captured and undo restores it.
repairs.verifyAfter: Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName DirectPlay is re-run and must report Enabled. Whether the game then launches is something only the game can answer, and the result says so rather than claiming the game is fixed.

buildApplicabilityNote: schemaVersion 3 adds three fields to EVERY repair entry so the catalog can finally say WHERE a repair applies, not just what it runs: minBuild (inclusive Windows build floor, null = no floor), maxBuild (inclusive ceiling, null = no ceiling, used when a mechanism was REMOVED in a later build), and generation ('any' | 'win10' | 'win11'). Before this the catalog had no way to express "this rung only exists on 23H2+" or "this is Windows 11 only", so 'repair.ps1 -Action list' returned an identical list on 21H2, 25H2, Windows 10 and Server, and every build-specific rung would have had to be hacked in as special-case code. repair.ps1 evaluates the three fields against the machine's CurrentBuildNumber and stamps every listed repair with applicable / notApplicableReason; a repair that does not apply here is still LISTED (so the user can see the rung exists and why it is unavailable) and 'run' refuses it with exit code 3 and errorCode 'not-applicable-on-this-build' unless -Force is given. applicable:null means the build could not be read — "could not determine", which also refuses, because running a build-gated repair on an unknown build is fixing blind. All three fields must be present on every entry even when their value is null; 'repair.ps1 -Action selftest' fails if any is missing, so the gate can never be silently forgotten on the next repair added. Most entries are minBuild:null / maxBuild:null / generation:'any' on purpose — sfc, DISM, chkdsk, the netsh resets, the Windows Update reset and the optional features all work on Windows 10 as well as 11, and marking them win11-only would drop a working capability rather than describe one.
stateLocationNote: RUNTIME STATE LOCATION. The repair ledger and the file backups live in %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state (repairs-ledger.json, and backups\ beside it) — the same folder engine/engine.ps1 uses, and deliberately NOT inside the install tree. A per-machine install under %ProgramFiles%, a read-only or network copy, Controlled Folder Access, or a OneDrive Known-Folder-Move profile all make <install>\data\state unwritable, and an engine that cannot write its ledger cannot undo anything (doctrine rule 3). Five repairs here are usable without administrator rights (wu-repair-reinstall, store-cache-reset, store-reregister, shell-restart, temp-clean) and a standard user could not run any of them while state lived in the install tree; the qmgr*.dat and print-spool backups that are the only recovery path for the reversible:false repairs lived there too, where an uninstall destroys them. A ledger written by an earlier version into <install>\data\state is COPIED to the new location on first use and the original is left exactly where it was — nothing is moved and nothing is deleted. If the state folder cannot be created or written, a run ABORTS before it mutates anything rather than proceeding unrecorded, and 'repair.ps1 -Action ledger' reports errorCode 'ledger-unreadable' rather than an empty ledger: a file that could not be read is never rendered as 'no repairs recorded'. OVERRIDE: if the environment variable FRAMEFORGE_STATE_DIR is set to a non-blank path, THAT directory is the state root instead - it holds repairs-ledger.json and backups\ exactly as %LOCALAPPDATA%\FrameForge\state otherwise would. It exists so the engine test suite can sandbox repair state: New-FFSandbox copies engine\ and data\ to %TEMP% and relies on the engine resolving everything relative to its own location, which an absolute %LOCALAPPDATA% path defeated - a suite run wrote to the invoking user's REAL ledger while the SAFETY assertions checked a sandbox path the engine could never write. A set-but-unusable override is a hard reported failure; it NEVER falls back to %LOCALAPPDATA%, because a caller that believes it is sandboxed must not be able to write the real ledger by accident. When the override is in force the v1 install-tree migration is skipped, and 'repair.ps1 -Action ledger' reports both the resolved root (stateDir) and where it came from (stateDirSource: 'localappdata' | 'env-override' | 'temp-fallback').
localeNote: PORTABILITY (doctrine rule 2). No repair in this catalog decides an OUTCOME by matching English text any more. Where prose is the only thing a tool prints, the parse is layered exactly like image.ps1's language detection — exit code or structured source first, the DOCUMENTED English-only text parse as a middle rung, and an honest 'could not determine' last — and the honest-unknown branch is always reported as NOT completed rather than allowed to fall through to success. Concretely: sfc's result is read from its exit code, then the [SR] markers in %SystemRoot%\Logs\CBS\CBS.log that were written AT OR AFTER that scan started (the locale-independent rung, and the same order and the same marker set engine/health.ps1 uses, so the probe and the repair cannot grade one machine differently), then its DOCUMENTED English-only console text, and a result none of those can establish now FAILS the run instead of reporting fixed:true; whether chkdsk scheduled an offline check is read from BootExecute and the volume dirty bit, and when neither can be read the step says so instead of asserting that nothing was scheduled; 'netsh int ip reset' is judged by its exit code plus whether it actually wrote its reset log, not by the word 'resetting'; activation success is read from SoftwareLicensingProduct.LicenseStatus, the same structured source the health probe uses; the Windows Time peer list and sync type are read from HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\Parameters, and the last successful sync from System event id 35, so neither detection nor undo depends on w32tm's localized labels. Command paths in whatItRuns use the %SystemRoot% / %ProgramData% / %TEMP% tokens rather than C:\Windows, because Windows is not always installed on C: and the catalog must document the command that actually runs. CASE FOLDING: PowerShell's -match, -notmatch, -like, -replace and -split fold case with the CURRENT CULTURE, not invariantly (only -eq / -ieq are invariant). Measured under tr-TR on PS 5.1: ('info' -match 'INFO') is False, ('CLIENT' -like 'Client*') is False, ('FILE' -replace 'file','X') returns 'FILE' unchanged, and an inline (?i) does not help. engine/repair.ps1 therefore pins the thread to the invariant culture as its first statement (before any pattern is compiled and cached) AND routes every text parse that decides an outcome through an explicitly CultureInvariant matcher, so no verdict in this catalog depends on the machine's regional settings.
managedMachineNote: ENVIRONMENT. Three signals decide whether this machine's update pipeline is managed by someone other than the user, and the engine reads all three before touching anything: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WindowsUpdate (WUServer / WUStatusServer / UseWUServer / TargetGroup), HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Enrollments\*\ProviderID (MDM/Intune), and Win32_ComputerSystem.PartOfDomain. They are recorded in the ledger before-state as wuPolicy and surfaced by 'repair.ps1 -Action preflight' as managementState / managementNote BEFORE anything runs. On a managed machine wu-reset does NOT clear the WinHTTP proxy (on a corporate network that proxy is the machine's only route to updates, and clearing it would break Windows Update, the Store and activation rather than repair them — and this repair is reversible:false, so there would be no automatic way back) and does NOT delete the WSUS client identity (that forces a full re-registration against the WSUS server named by policy, not against Microsoft, and makes the machine vanish from the WSUS console until it reports in — an administrator action, not a user one). Both steps report the refusal by name instead of executing silently. ntp-resync refuses on a domain member rather than taking it off the domain time hierarchy, because a clock that drifts past the Kerberos five-minute tolerance costs the user logon, shares and intranet access. Nothing here reads, writes, or removes Group Policy itself.
repairLadderNote: The system-files ladder, cheapest rung first: sfc-scannow (5-15 min) — dism-restorehealth (DISM then SFC) — wu-repair-reinstall (Settings > Recovery > "Fix problems using Windows Update" > Reinstall now: one reboot, no ISO, Windows 11 23H2+ only) — and only then the full ISO in-place repair in data/image-repair.json (30-90 min, two or three reboots, consent contract, BitLocker rails). wu-repair-reinstall belongs BELOW the ISO in-place repair in any UI that renders the ladder: it is the cheaper option to try first on the builds that have it. It is guided rather than scripted because the flow has no documented CLI. On Windows 11 21H2 (22000) and 22H2 (22621) it is listed with applicable:false and a reason naming the build, so the absence is explained rather than silent.
